§ 46-51. Proctors 

Examinations shall be conducted under the care and supervision of proctors appointed by the Bureau. At least one person of each sex will be appointed per examination room to take care of any emergency that may occur. 

§ 46-52. Examination centers 

Examination centers should be kept free from noise and interference of any kind. 

§ 46-53. Timepiece 

A clock should be affixed in a visible place in the examination premises. 

§ 46-54. Seats 

Seats for candidates should be placed so that all manner of communication will be avoided. 116

Ch. T.18 § 46-60 

 § 46-55. Admission 

The admission card sent to each candidate is indispensable for access to the examination room. This card is placed in an envelope to which a photograph of the candidate has been attached. The photograph should under no circumstance be detached from the envelope or the right to take the examination may be forfeited. 

On its presentation at the door of the examination room for the purpose of personal identification, the admission card should be perforated and returned to the candidate. The candidate takes his place and places his admission card on his desk. 

After the examination has begun, the examiner in charge will go around the room and perforate the card on the space opposite the corresponding subject.

The candidates must keep their admission cards, giving them to the examiner in charge of their last examination. Examination proctors are responsible for the compliance with this provision. § 46-56. Attendance at examinations

Punctuality is essential to those who administer and to those who take examinations. No candidate will be admitted into the examination room later than thirty minutes after the test has started and no candidate will be allowed to leave the room while the examination is in progress. 

§ 46-57. Subjects 

Candidates will be examined only in those subjects specified in their admission cards. § 46-58. Visits to examination rooms

Proctors will not permit visitors to the rooms where examinations are being held. 

§ 46-59. Duration of examinations 

The duration of the test period is specified in the schedule. This period of time may not be extended after the signal to stop work has been given.

The candidates must leave the room at the end of each period unless they must take a test scheduled right after. § 46-60. Dishonest conduct during examinations

Any person caught in a flagrant act of dishonesty, imposture or fraud will immediately be dismissed from the examination 117

T.§ 46-60 Ch. 3 

premises. Anyone committing fraud or imposture in connection with his examinations will lose his examinations and all his year examinations will be cancelled. Examination proctors should report all cases of dishonest conduct. Their report will be final and no attention shall be given to applications for reconsideration of the matter. 

§ 46-61. Examination material 

No candidate shall be permitted to have in his possession books, papers, blotters, etc. Candidates shall not be permitted to use their own note paper; all work should be done on paper supplied by the examiners. Whenever necessary, maps, charts, logarithm tables, etc. will be provided. 

§ 46-62. Written test 

The test may be written out either in ink or pencil. Erasures shall not be made. Corrections may be made by crossing out wrong words or answers. Only official paper supplied by the examiner may be used. § 46-63. Answers in excess of those required 

Candidates should answer only the number of questions required.

Answers in excess of those required will receive no credit on correction. 

§ 46-64. Explanation of questions 

Under no circumstance will the examiner explain or criticize any question in the test. The student is responsible for the interpretation of all questions. In case of typographical errors, the examiner will address the entire group, directing necessary corrections. 

In such a case, the examiner should make a written report to the director explaining the corrections made. This report should accompany the examination papers. 

Examiners should see that all maps, charts, tables, figures, etc. (except those to be supplied according to instructions) are removed from the examination premises. 

§ 46-65. Comments on examination papers 

Proctors are not allowed to make any comments on examination papers that are handed out to candidates. § 46-66. Absences from examinations

Candidates may not leave the presence of the examiner while 118

Ch. T.18 § 47-2 

taking a test. In case of urgent necessity the candidate may leave accompanied by an examiner. If a candidate leaves the presence of the examiner, his examination for the particular subject that he is taking will be declared ended.

§ 47-2. Subjects 

In accordance with this provision, examinations will be offered in English, Spanish, Mathematics, Social Studies and Natural Sci ence.

The English and Spanish tests will include exercises in reading comprehension, language, composition, vocabulary and letter writing. The social studies and natural science tests will determine the candidates' ability to analyze and interpret selections related to the content of these subjects. The difficulty levels of the selections will equal that of the content of regular high school subjects, such as General History, History of Puerto Rico, History of 

United States, General Science, Biology, Chemistry and Physics.

The Mathematics test will determine the candidates' ability to solve arithmetic problems, especially those related to the common 119

T.§ 47-2 Ch. 3 

practical business transactions, and will in addition include exercises that require a basic knowledge of elementary algebra and plane geometry.

By virtue of their nature and content these tests constitute measures of intelligence, intellectual maturity and basic knowledges of the candidates taking them. § 47-3. Requisites for admission 

Interested applicants should file with this office: (1) An eighth grade diploma; a ninth grade diploma or the official transcript of high school work approved by the applicant; (2) The applicant's birth certificate; (3) A certificate of good conduct signed by one of the following: a municipal judge, a local police lieutenant, a priest or minister of the church, the employer or chief of the office where the applicant works; and (4) Two 21½" x 22" photos.

§ 57-1. Preamble 

The direction and guidance of public education in Puerto Rico is the function of the Secretary of Education working through the Department of Education according to the dispositions of the 

Constitution and laws of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico. 

The objective of the schools, private as well as public, is to provide for the development of citizens who are conscious of their privileges and obligations as members of a democratic society. 

Source. §§ 57-1 to 57-14: Regulation for accreditation of private elementary and secondary schools already established or that may be established in Puerto Rico and which seek official recognition for their educational program, promulgated by Secretary of Education, app. Jan. 8, 1959, eff. upon com pliance with Act June 30, 1957, No. 112; 3 L.P.R.A. §§ 1041 to 

1059. Filed with Secretary of State Jan. 16, 1959; File No. 549.

Authority. Act Aug. 22, 1958, No. 2; 18 L.P.R.A. § 57. 

§ 57-2. Definition of terms 

The terms and expressions used in this subchapter will have 122

Ch. T.18 § 57-4 

the meaning that is given below unless the context clearly indicates a different connotation. (1) "Private school." This will be understood to mean any elementary or secondary school and any vocational or special school whose support does not depend upon the property or funds of the 

Commonwealth of Puerto Rico. 

(2) "Accredited private school." A private school which has complied with the standards for accreditation which have been set by this subchapter and thereby has been accredited by the Secre tary of Education. 

(3) "Secretary." The Secretary of Education. 

(4) "Department." The Department of Education. 

(5) "Regulations." The current regulations regarding the certification of teachers, administered by the Secretary of Education. (6) "Director." The school official in charge of its administration and supervision. 

§ 57-3. Application for accreditation 

Any private elementary, secondary, or special school that so desires may seek official recognition of its educational program in the form of accreditation by making formal application to that effect to the Secretary of Education. 

§ 57-4. Standards 

(a) Any private school interested in securing accreditation must first have achieved the following standards: (1) It must have a well-defined philosophy geared to the principles and ideals which foster a full and democratic way of life and a desire for education. (2) It must have prepared a working plan based on the educational problems, interests, and needs of the students and the community. (3) It must have a faculty whose teachers have a professional and academic preparation that measures up to the requirements for certification or licensing of teachers by the Secretary of Education according to the dispositions of Law No. 94, passed on June 

21, 1955 and known as "the Law for Certification of Teachers, 18

L.P.R.A. §§ 260 to 273, and in accordance with the Regulations regarding Certification of Teachers [sec. 261-1 et seq. of this title] 

which the Secretary of Education has proclaimed. When the circumstances justify, provisional teachers who do not fulfill the 123

T.§ 57-4 Ch. 3 

requirements with respect to preparation and experience may be employed provided that they fulfill the requirements as set forth in the Regulations for the Certification of Provisional Teachers 

[sec. 261-29 et seq. of this title]. (4) The school calendar must indicate the school days, holidays, and dates for the beginning and ending of the school year. 

It should be understood that any change in this calendar must be reported to the Secretary of Education prior to the date on which it is to take effect. (5) Standards comparable to those set for the public schools by the Department of Education with respect to the minimum requirements for graduation from the elementary, junior high, and high schools must be maintained. (6) The following documents must be kept available in the files: (A) The academic and professional records of the teaching and administrative personnel. (B) Files on students. These records must be permanent and must include the following information: (i) Academic achievement of the student, (ii) Results of any standardized tests that the student may have taken, (iii) Personal traits, interests, abilities, etc. (C) Circular letters, memorandums, and correspondence with the superintendent of schools. (D) Circular letters, memorandums, and correspondence with the central office of the Department of Education. (b) The organization standards for accredited private schools must correspond to those set for the public schools by the Department of Education with respect to the following: (1) Length and frequency of class periods, (2) Number of pupils per class. (c) The building or buildings in which the classrooms are located must fulfill the following minimum requirements: (1) The school must be situated on a large plot of ground which furnishes facilities for recreation and guarantees the safety of the students. (2) It must comply with the requirements for ventilation, light, and sanitary facilities as established by the Department of 

Health regulations. 

124

Ch. T.18 § 57-5 

(3) It must fulfill the minimum requirements for fire prevention set by the state fire department. 

(4) All rooms used by the school classrooms, libraries, laboratories, shops, etc. must have access to yards or balconies which make for rapid exit of the students in case of emergency. 

(5) Size of the classrooms: 

(A) The classrooms must provide a minimum space of 18 square feet per pupil. (B) The domestic science and industrial arts classrooms must approximate a size of 24 feet wide by 42 feet long. (6) The school must provide space for the principal's office. (d) The equipment in use in these schools must meet the following standards: 

(1) Classroom equipment: 

(A) Satisfactory seats in sufficient numbers for the assignment of one to every pupil. (B) An adequate number of well-located blackboards. (C) A desk and chair for the teacher in every classroom. 

(2) The classrooms for domestic science, industrial arts, commercial education, and science laboratories must be furnished with the equipment and materials necessary for the teaching of these subjects. § 57-5. Procedures for obtaining accreditation (a) Any private school interested in applying for and obtaining official recognition of its educational program (accreditation) must make formal application to the office of the superintendent of schools of the school district in which the school is located, which application must be accompanied by the documents which are specified later in this subchapter. (b) The application for accreditation must state: (1) The name of the owner of the school or the name of the institution fostering it 

(2) The official name of the school 

(3) The length of time that it has been in operation (4) The philosophy and basic aims of the school (5) The language in which the teaching is carried on (6) The kind of organization (7) The requirements for admission (8) Tuition, deposits, monthly payments, and other fees. 125

T.§ 57-6 Ch. 3 

 § 57-6. Documents 

Documents which must accompany the application are: (1) Plan of organization of the school which shows: (A) the grades (B) the subjects (C) the school schedule, including the length and frequency of class periods (D) enrollment by grade, by subject, by group, and total enrollment (E) faculty and teaching program of each teacher (F) administrative personnel (2) A list of the teaching personnel showing preparation and experience (3) A sketch of every floor of the building or buildings which the school occupies showing (A) play space inside and outside the building (B) dimensions of every room (C) the number and size of the wash rooms and toilets (D) drinking water facilities (E) space devoted to first aid service. (F) office space (4) In case of new buildings, a permit-to-use issued by the 

Planning Board (5) A description of the equipment that the school provides (A) office equipment (B) equipment for classrooms and for commercial education rooms (C) equipment for science laboratories and libraries (D) equipment for industrial arts workshops and domestic science rooms (6) A bibliography of the textbooks used in each subject (7) A school calendar showing the dates for beginning and ending the school year and the holidays. 

§ 57-7. Granting of certificate 

After the aforementioned documents have been submitted, the 

Secretary of Education will study the same through his authorized representatives, who will visit the school in order to observe the condition and functioning of the institution. As a result of this action, the general supervisor and the superintendent of the school district in which the school is located will submit reports to the 126

Ch. T.18 § 57-9 

Secretary, who, after due consideration of the same, will render his decision to the school concerned regarding the application for accreditation submitted by it. 

The certificate of accreditation will be granted only for the courses and grades which have been the object of study and favorable consideration. Any subsequent amplification of the educational program of a previously accredited institution which involves new courses or grades will subject the institution once again to an accreditation procedure with respect to these added courses or grades and will result in appropriate amendments to the original certificate of accreditation. 

§ 57-8. Revocation 

The certificate of accreditation issued by the Secretary to a particular school is subject to revocation in the event that in his judgment the school is not complying with the dispositions of these regulations. § 57-9. Standards for maintaining accreditation 

In order to maintain the accreditation once it has been granted by the Secretary of Education, the accredited school must: (1) Meet all the standards set for the original accreditation. (2) Submit to the Department through the office of the Superintendent of Schools of the district in which the school is located within the first fifteen days from the beginning of the new school year the following documents duly executed: (A) Plans of organization of the school program. (B) The calendar for the school year showing the dates for its beginning and ending and the holidays which will be observed by the institution. (C) A list of the administrative and teaching personnel showing the academic preparation and professional experience of each one of the members of this group.

These documents, once they have been approved by the Secretary of Education, will constitute evidence that the accreditation granted originally continues to be in effect. (3) Other documents which must be submitted to the Department of Education are the following: (A) Notice of any change or alteration in the program of studies and the schedule as soon as it occurs. (B) Notice of any change in the administration and teaching personnel as soon as it occurs. 127

T.§ 57-9 Ch. 3 

(C) Any other report which the department may require from the school. 

§ 57-10. Correspondence 

It should be understood that all official correspondence between the Department of Education and the school must be carried on through the office of the superintendent of schools of the district in which the school is located. 

§ 57-11. Summer courses 

Accredited private schools that wish to organize accredited summer courses will be guided by such regulations for these courses as the Secretary of Education may establish. 

§ 57-12. Local supervision 

The superintendent of schools or his representative will periodically visit the accredited private schools located in his district and will see to it that the standards for accreditation set by this subchapter are maintained. 

§ 57-13. Special private schools 

The Secretary will approve separate and different standards for the special private schools, with the understanding that the provisions of this subchapter which are not in conflict with such standards will likewise be applicable to this special type of school. 

§ 57-14. Effectiveness 

This subchapter, upon being approved and adopted by the Secretary, will take effect as soon as the provisions of Law No. 112, passed on June 30, 1957 [3 L.P.R.A. §§ 1041 to 1059], and known as the Law concerning Regulations for 1958, have been complied with.

Preamble. Regulation No. 99 contained the following pre amble: "Recent studies as to the problem of barefooted children who attend the public schools of Puerto Rico show the large number who lack the means for acquiring shoes. In order to solve this problem at once, on June 13, 1955, the Legislature approved Act No. 66 [18 L.P.R.A. § 58], that provides funds and stipulates the way of using them to that effect.

"This Act empowers the Secretary of Education to 'make and put into effect rules and regulations for the fair distribution of the shoes acquired for the purposes of this act.' 

In view thereof, the Secretary of Education promulgates the following . 

Circular Letter No. 10. Circular Letter No. 10, Aug. 23, 

1955, addressed to school superintendents by the Secretary of

Education, gave notice of the shoe fund, requested a survey of shoe needs, provided a standard for selection of applicants, and urged formation of local agencies. 

§ 58-2. Administration 

A general administrator appointed by the Secretary of Education to work in the central office of the Department of Education, and a local organization appointed by the superintendent of schools in every district, will be in charge of the administration of the shoe program. 129

T.§ 58-2 Ch. 3 

The duties, functions, and responsibilities of the general administrator are the following: (1) To obtain from the superintendents of schools reports concerning the school children who lack the means of acquiring shoes. 

These reports are to be prepared during the first three weeks of the school term, using the forms prescribed to that effect. (2) To study in detail the reports from the school districts and to make a summary of them so as to determine the annual cost of the program. (3) To assign the corresponding funds to each school district according to the needs informed and based on the income available. (4) To require the holding of an auction for the purchase of shoes and to establish due specifications for same, according to the funds available and their proportional distribution among the districts. (5) To orient and guide the work of the local organizations. (6) To encourage campaigns and activities for the acquisition of gifts and to obtain cooperation from the municipal authorities. (7) To take care of the correspondence, to investigate complaints and claims, and to prepare forms for the various phases of the program. (8) To give the public information on the development of the program, using the various means of publicity. (9) To prepare reports for the Secretary of Education and other authorities related to the work of the program. § 58-3. Local organizations 

The local organization designated by the superintendent of schools in each district will consist of the number of members he deems fit. From the teaching and administrative staff in his district, the superintendent of schools will select those who, according to his judgment, are most capable and who will render their services voluntarily to bring about the noble purpose the program pursues.

The functions, duties, and responsibilities of the local organization will be the following: (1) To direct the preparation of reports requested by the Department of Education concerning the public school students who lack the means of acquiring shoes. (2) To examine, investigate, and classify, by order of deserving preferment, the cases of students who request shoes or who will 130

Ch. T.18 § 58-4 

profit from the program and to prepare four lists of the cases examined and classified thus, that is: 

A list of girls from the urban zone. 

A list of girls from the rural zone. 

A list of boys from the urban zone. 

A list of boys from the rural zone. (3) To organize the local distribution of shoes and to establish appropriate and uniform methods for delivery of shoes to the students. (4) To plan and supervise the collection of the sum of 50 cents that students should pay for each pair of shoes and to send the sum total of the proceeds of such sales to the Department of Education. The remittance should be made by money order or check payable to the Secretary of the Treasury, together with the accredited receipts of the delivery of shoes to the students, signed by them and their parents or guardians. If necessary, there will be a receiving officer in each district in charge of these collections and remittances. (5) To prepare and send to the Department of Education an itemized report of each distribution of shoes that has taken place in the district. The form for this report will be furnished by the general administrator. (6) To organize and put into practice campaigns and activities for the acquisition of gifts. (7) To prepare and to furnish the general administrator with any other report he or she may request. § 58-4. Requirements and conditions of applicants

The benefits of the shoe program will be granted to applicants who meet the following requirements and conditions, and according to the order established by the local organizations, as to the merits of each case: (1) To be a bona-fide student of a public elementary, junior high, senior high, or vocational school in the urban or rural zone. (2) Lack of means to purchase shoes, due to orphanage, desertion, or circumstances such as unemployment, illness, or insufficient income of parents or guardians. (3) Payment of 50 cents for each pair of shoes as provided by law. (4) Promise to continue in school, that is, not to leave unless it be for justified reasons. This promise is to be endorsed by parents or guardians. 131

T.§ 58-4 Ch. 3 

 Amendments. Section was amended by Memorandum No. 

72, March 19, 1956. 

§ 58-5. Purchase of shoes 

The purchase of shoes will be effected through auctions which will be held when the general administrator of the program makes requisitions. These requisitions will have all the necessary specifications as to the shoes to be purchased, such as quality, durability, style, price, quantity, conditions of easy delivery in the school districts, and any other convenient conditions. A committee appointed by the Secretary of Education will be in charge of each auction.

The acceptance of the bid will be made according to the recommendations of the general administrator of the program. Once the bid is accepted, the Division of Finance will issue the corresponding orders and will award the contract to the successful bidder. $ 58-6. Effectiveness

§ 95-1. Legal basis 

This division is adopted by virtue of the powers conferred on the Secretary of Education in an Act of March 12, 1903, as amended, 3 L.P.R.A. §§ 141-142 and Act No. 139 of June 29, 1969 [18 L.P.R.A. §§ 91 to 99], which empower the State Board of Education to approve regulations.

Source. Sections 95-1 to 95-13: Regulations for Students in the Public School System, app. by the Secretary of Education and the State Board of Education June 15, 1971; eff. immediately upon approval. Filed with the Secretary of State

Preamble. The regulations, set out in this division, contained the following preamble: "The people of Puerto Rico recognize the fundamental importance of education in the preservation and enjoyment of a democratic life and the training of adequately prepared citizens who will be responsible for and respectful of the rights and ethical values of all human beings. "Our constitution establishes the right to education within certain limits and our Legislature authorizes and orders the Secretary of Education to establish and maintain a system of public schools in Puerto Rico, and to establish the regulations which he deems necessary for the effective discharge of his office. 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.1

T.§ 95-1 Ch. 6 

EDUCATION-PUBLIC SCHOOLS 

"For the maintenance of this school system it is essential to foster within the compass of the school a climate that will facilitate the educative process and will lead to the full development of the student's personality and the strengthening of respect for the rights of man and the fundamental freedoms. "In order to lead our school population towards the achievement of these objectives, these regulations are adopted establishing the rights and duties of students as members of the school community of the public school system of Puerto Rico and to provide rules that will promote a better living together among students and with teachers, principals, and other school personnel." 

§ 95-2. Applicability 

This division will apply to every student enrolled in the elementary, secondary, vocational, technical, or special schools or who participate in any program or activity under the direction and/or jurisdiction of the Department of Education and will be called "Regulations for Students in the Public School System". 

§ 95-3. Definitions of terms 

The following words and phrases, as used in this division, have the meanings hereinafter established: (a) "Regulations", the present body of this division. (b) "Secretary", the Secretary of Education. (c) "Superintendent of Schools", official in charge of administering a school district. (d) "School Principal", official directly in charge of the supervision and administration of a school or teaching unit. (e) "Teacher in charge", individual who directs a school of a teaching unit by special assignment. (f) "Teacher", all teaching personnel in charge of groups of students or offering them special services. (g) "Student", every student enrolled in a public school offering elementary, secondary, vocational, technical, or special education, or participating in any other program or activity under the direction and/or jurisdiction of the Department of Education. (h) "Parent or guardian", includes the father, mother, tutor, or other person having parental authority, custody and/or responsibility for a student. (i) "School", any building and/or structure, including the lands where it is located and all its annexed properties, under the total, 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 

134.2

Ch. T.18 § 95-3 

COMMONWEALTH BOARD 

partial, or temporary, control or jurisdiction of the Department of Education. (j) "Accrediting body", refers to the group of persons who study and certify student organizations. (k) "Student organizations", groups of students certified as bona fide by the school authorities or the Secretary of Education. (1) "Good behavior", attitude of respect towards all school personnel and properties, as well as towards students, parents, visitors, and the community in general, and the compliance with the school policies and regulations, and instructions received from teachers. (m) "Transfer", moving a student from one school to another either within the same school district or from one district to another. (n) "Political partisan activity", an activity sponsored by political entities, organizations or parties, or by any person or group of persons whose actions are aimed at fostering certain ideas or methods as to how the political order should be organized and directed, or having as a goal the advancement of their own purposes and ends. 

(n-1) (Corresponds to Spanish version ñ) "Religious sec tarian activity", an activity whose objectives are related to any sect or religion. (0) "Punctual attendance", presence of the students in their classrooms at the appointed time for their school work. (p) "Regular attendance", daily presence of students in classes, activities or exercises offered during the school year. (q) "Student strikes", abandonment of or absence from classes, or refusal to participate in them by common agreement of the students with the purpose of imposing certain conditions on teachers, school authorities, and other school personnel in order to compel them to accept the conditions imposed by the students, or to achieve some other objective. (r) "Student pickets", public demonstrations made by one or more students in common agreement to intimidate or bring pressure to bear upon their teachers, school authorities, and other school personnel, in order to compel them to accept the conditions imposed by the students or to attain some other objective. (s) "Defaming", the act of exposing any person or institution by any means of communication to public hatred, scorn, or ridicule by impugning his honesty, integrity, virtue, or reputation. 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.3

T.§ 95-3 

Ch. 6

EDUCATION-PUBLIC SCHOOLS 

(t) "Obscene material", any material-handwritten, photographed, or in some manner printed or reproduced-which contains images whose nature and presentation taken together tend to attract or arouse interest in nudity and sex, and which are of a lewd or vicious character offensive to the moral criteria and good customs prevailing in the community, and which are wanting in artistic, literary, educative or social value. 

§ 95-4. Student rights 

(a) The fundamental right of every student in the public schools of Puerto Rico is to receive the benefit of an education leading to the full development of his personality and to the strengthening of his respect for human rights, as well as to the enjoyment of basic freedoms. Education in the public schools in the elementary and secondary level will be entirely free, unrestricted, and nonsectarian, and will provide equal educational opportunities to all. (b) The student will be entitled to express his opinions freely, as well as to dissent from the views of his teachers. The exercise of this right does not relieve the student of the duty of complying with the appropriate requirements of the course or courses of study. (c) The student will be entitled to have his school work carefully and fairly rated by his teachers, on the basis of criteria officially established by the Department of Education. 

(d) The student passing each one of the courses making up the teaching program will be entitled to the issuance of the corresponding credential in the form of a diploma or other document accrediting the satisfactory completion of the courses. The student will be entitled to receive report cards concerning his school work as well as his deportment in school from the school authorities. (e) The student will be entitled to present his grievances and to plead his rights in due form whenever he deems it necessary, and to present individual or collective petitions to the proper authorities. The school must establish administrative machinery to consider the complaints and petitions of the students. (f) Students are entitled to organize associations freely, but the latter will be able to function in the schools only when they are recognized and registered by the school administration. (g) The student will be entitled to request and to be granted an administrative hearing to determine the fairness or propriety of any sanction or punishment involving suspension of the student 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.4

Ch. T.18 § 95-6 

COMMONWEALTH BOARD 

for more than 30 days, following the procedure established by subsec. (e) of sec. 95-9 of this division. 

§ 95-5. Duties of the students 

(a) Students of the public schools will attend classes punctually and regularly, will devote themselves to study and to other assignments with a due sense of responsibility, and will observe good behavior during class hours as well as during recess and other school activities. If they find it impossible to attend classes punctually and/or regularly, because of illness or other cause, they should justify their absence or tardiness according to the rules established by the school. (b) Students enrolled in the public schools will attend the length of time necessary to finish each of the courses of the study program according to the plan in force. Attendance of students in elementary school will be compulsory as far as the resources of the 

State permit. (c) It will be the duty of every student to follow the guidance and instructions of the teachers in the educative process according to curricular standards. (d) Every student in the public schools shall abstain from causing damage to school property, equipment, and every kind of school material. (e) Students should observe good behavior in school, as well as outside the school premises, and will not engage in any act that will interrupt the quiet, affect the safety, and/or alter the normal operation of the school work, or do anything which will harm the good name of the school system. (f) The clothes and personal appearance of the student should be in line with the accepted community standards, as they are established in each school district by the Council of Supervision, after consultation with parents and students and the approval of the Secretary of Education, and they shall not be of such a nature as to cause detrimental reactions to the atmosphere of study and discipline that should prevail in the classroom. 

§ 95-6. Student organizations 

(a) The Superintendent of Schools will establish an accrediting body for student organizations in each school district. (b) Only student organizations whose objective is the intellectual, cultural, vocational, technical, moral, social and/or civic 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.5

T.§ 95-6 

Ch. 6

EDUCATION-PUBLIC SCHOOLS 

development of its members will be recognized with all the rights that such official recognition implies. (c) No recognition will be granted to any organization with political-partisan or religious-sectarian purposes, as the latter are defined in this division, or to those establishing discrimination of a racial, social, economic, religious, or political nature for the admission of members. (d) A student or group of students interested in organizing a student organization should submit a written application to the School Principal. If the petitioners belong to more than one school, the petition should be submitted to the Superintendent of Schools. (e) A student or a group of students interested in obtaining recognition for a student organization should submit a written application to the accrediting body, through the School Principal, or through the Superintendent of Schools when the petitioners belong to more than one school. The application for recognition should state the purposes of the organization and other required information. (f) The accrediting body will study the application and notify its decision in writing within a term of not more than 30 days after the date of the filing of the application. If said body does not act within that time the application will be considered approved. (g) If the accrediting body denies the application for the authorization of a student organization, the affected students may ask the same accrediting body for a reconsideration within a period of 10 days after denial. The accrediting body must decide on the application for reconsideration within a term of 5 days after having received it. If the original decision is upheld, the affected students may apply for the revision of the decision by the Superintendent of Schools, who will make a decision within a term of not more than 

5 days. (h) If the Superintendent of Schools confirms the denial of the accrediting body, the affected students may apply for a review of the decision of the Superintendent of Schools within a term of 10 days after receiving said decision. The Secretary of Education will make the final determination on the application. (i) Every organization will have a teacher advisor who will be selected by mutual agreement between a recognized organization and the School Principal. When there is no agreement between the parties, the teacher advisor will be selected by the Superintendent of Schools from available teachers in the same school. 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.6

Ch. T.18 § 95-7 

COMMONWEALTH BOARD 

(j) Meetings of accredited student organizations should be previously authorized by the School Principal or the person assigned by him, and notification given to the advisor. If the advisor cannot attend, he should inform the Principal so that he may appoint a substitute advisor. The teacher advisor or his substitute will have the duty of attending these meetings in order to discharge his duties as advisor to the organization. No meeting will be valid if it has not been previously authorized by the School Principal and notification given to the organization advisor. Unauthorized meetings will be considered a violation of this division. (k) The accrediting body may revoke the authorization granted to any organization acting counter to the policies established in this division, the school laws, and other such divisions governing the public school system of Puerto Rico. None of the provisions of this section will limit the authority possessed by the Secretary of Education to examine, ratify, or revoke any decision of the accrediting body, the School Principal, or the Superintendent of 

Schools. 

§ 95-7. School discipline, 

The following actions constitute violations of the institutional order and they are punishable with disciplinary sanctions: (a) Organizing, instigating, inciting, directing, and/or participating in student strikes within the school or outside the school. (b) Organizing, instigating, inciting, directing and/or participating in student pickets on school grounds and in the buildings. 

Disciplinary action will also be applied if said acts are carried out outside the school grounds and buildings if they affect the institutional order. (c) Impeding or trying to impede students, teachers, school authorities, and other school personnel or visitors from entering and/or attending schools. (d) Using loud speakers within the school premises without written authorization of the School Principal, or outside the school. premises if the institutional order is affected. (e) Organizing in the school, activities of religious-sectarian, political-partisan or any activity of this nature sponsored by political parties or entities, or by any student organization, whose acts are directed towards the sponsoring of certain ideas, ideologies and/or methods of organizing or directing the political order or having as an end the advancement of their own purposes or ends. 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.7

T.§ 95-7

Ch. T.18 § 95-9 

COMMONWEALTH BOARD § 95-8. Sanctions 

The violation of the preceding prohibitions may result in the adoption of some of the following measures: (a) Admonition. (b) Subjection to a probational status without suspension from classes for a definite period. (c) Transfer to another school in the same school district. (d) Transfer to another school district. (e) Suspension for a definite period according to further provisions in this division. (f) Dismissal from the school system. 

§ 95-9. Norms and procedures for imposition of sanctions 

(a) In the first instance, the teacher or the School Director will deal with acts involving improper behavior by students and may admonish them, and when he deems it necessary may send written admonitions to the students' parents. He may also refer the students for guidance and help to the social worker, where one is available, or to another teacher. (b) By means of an informal procedure, the School Principal, prior to an investigation and the opportunity to be heard, may suspend a student up to a maximum of 5 school days for a violation of any of the provisions of this division or other school laws and policies. The student and the parent or guardian should be informed through written communication of the imposed disciplinary sanction and the reasons therefor. The Superintendent of Schools may act in the first instance when in his judgment the case warrants it, following the informal procedure established above. (c) When the behavior observed by a student is of such a nature as to merit a sanction of a suspension of more than 5 school days and/or transfer to another school in the same district, the case should be referred to the Superintendent of Schools, who may, prior to the holding of an informal procedure, apply such sanctions as admonition, suspension for a maximum of 10 days, including the previous 5-day suspension, and/or transfer to another school within the school district. The parent or guardian of the student must be informed in writing of the imposed disciplinary sanction and the reasons therefor. (d) When the behavior of the student is of such a nature that it may warrant suspension for more than 10 days, transfer to another school district, imposition of probational status, or dismissal 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.9

T.18 95 

Ch. 6

EDUCATION-PUBLIC SCHOOLS 

from the school system, the Superintendent of Schools will refer the case to the Secretary of Education, who may extend the student's suspension for a maximum period of 30 days while the case is being decided. The Secretary of Education may apply any of the sanctions listed in sec. 95-8 of this division. (e) In a case that may involve suspension for more than 30 calendar days, or a penalty of greater severity, the Secretary of Education will inform the student and his parent or guardian of the charges against him and the length of time given to answering them. He will also be informed of his right to ask for and be granted an administrative hearing before a committee appointed by the Secretary of Education, in which at least one private citizen will be included. The student may appear in the hearing accompanied by his parent or guardian, and he may be assisted by legal counsel or an advisor, present evidence and confront the witnesses against him. An adequate record of the hearings will be taken, and it will not be necessary to follow the rules of evidence in force in law courts. The committee will render a report with the proper recommendations to the Secretary of Education, who will make the pertinent determination, which will be notified in writing to the student and his parent or guardian, and the lawyer or advisor who has represented him. If the Secretary of Education deems it advisable, the student will continue under suspension from classes during all the time taken to reach the final decision of his case. (f) Whenever he deems it necessary to protect the interests of the public school system, the Secretary of Education may summarily suspend a student for a period of no more than 30 days. 

During this period he must carry on an investigation and proceed to prefer charges, with the right to a hearing as provided in subsec. (e) of sec. 95-9 of this division, or to reinstate the student. If charges are preferred against the student, he will remain under suspension for the period of time necessary to reach a final decision of his case. (g) The sanction or sanctions imposed on a student should correspond to the gravity of his fault and, as far as possible, persuasive measures must be preferred before resort is made to sanctions. 

§ 95-10. Commencement and other activities 

(a) Commencement exercises constitute one of the official school activities. It is important that the exercises held on that day 1972 

Vol. 11, No. 4 134.10

Ch. T.18 § 95-11 

COMMONWEALTH BOARD 

should be school celebrations which express the spirit of the school and utilize the talent that it has helped to develop. Commencement exercises should tighten the bonds between the school and the community. (b) The following norms will be observed in the organization and celebration of these exercises: (1) Students, parents, teachers and school authorities will participate in commencement exercises. (2) The attire and other requirements should be adopted with the participation of students, parents, teachers and school principals, provided that conditions or requirements are of such a nature as not to impose economic hardships or hinder the participation of students in these exercises. (3) The celebration of these exercises should take place during the daytime and on the school premises, and exceptions to this norm must be authorized by the Superintendent of Schools. (4) The greatest care should be exercised in the selection of commencement speakers in order to avoid sectarian or partisan propaganda. Before proceeding to issue formal invitations, each school principal should submit to the Superintendent of Schools for his information and approval the name or names of appropriate persons to offer messages at the commencement exercises. Once the approval is received from the Superintendent of Schools the formal invitation shall be issued to the selected speaker. (5) The School Principal should submit the commencement program to the Superintendent of Schools for his approval. (c) Dances, outings, or any other activities held by the students. on the occasion of commencement may be sponsored by the school if they are approved and supervised by school authorities.

(a) Each school individually may establish internal rules which are not in conflict with this division or with legislation in force. (b) The use of school uniforms may be permitted, though it is not compulsory, if suggested by the students themselves and the Parent-Teacher Council of the school concerned. (c) Nothing contained in this division should be construed as limiting the authority of the Secretary of Education to initiate and adopt measures he may deem necessary to guarantee discipline in the schools and in its institutional activities. 1972

Subchapter 102. Transfer of School Buildings and Property to Commonwealth; Exceptions

DIVISION 1. USE OF SCHOOLHOUSES AND OTHER SCHOOL PROPERTIES FOR PRIVATE PURPOSES SECTIONS 

102-1. General rule 

102-2. Political, sectarian or commercial interests 

102-3. Dances 

102-4. Permission by superintendent; damages; expenses 102-5. 

Interference with school 

§ 102-1. General rule 

The law provides that the buildings and other school properties, whether they are the property of the Government or are rented, shall be placed at the service of the schools and shall at all times be available for school work. The law does not contain any provisions for granting of schools for purposes other than teaching. 

However, there are certain activities which clearly justify the schools in rendering their cooperation because they might be for the developing of culture or for the spreading of general welfare. 

It becomes necessary to fix the conditions under which the schools may be granted for these sort of activities, and this division responds to this necessity.

Source. §§ 102-1 to 102-5: Rules and regulations of Depart ment of Education, app. by Secretary of Education, Vol I, pp. 

48 to 50, "Use of Schoolhouses and other School Properties for Private Purposes", promulgated June 24, 1947, eff. July 

1, 1947. Filed with Secretary of State Sept. 28, 1957; File 

No. 344. 

Authority. Act Mar. 19, 1946, No. 76, p. 166; May 15, 1947, No. 472, p. 1060; 18 L.P.R.A. § 102. § 102-2. Political, sectarian or commercial interests

The use of schoolrooms and other school properties for purposes not in connection with the operation of the schools shall be limited to such activities which are not related to motives or purposes of political, sectarian or commercial character, since the public schools, which are supported with the funds from the whole community, shall be kept free from any acts that do not carry general interest, and especially those that might have as a purpose the defense or propaganda of political, religious or personal 135

T.§ 102-2 Ch. 7 

interests. The Secretary of Education should be consulted in case of doubt. 

§ 102-3. Dances 

The giving of dances in the school buildings, schoolrooms, school grounds and establishments, being the property of the Government or rented, are positively prohibited. § 102-4. Permission by superintendent; damages; expenses

The school superintendent shall be the only one permitted to grant permission for the use of the school buildings and other school properties, for purposes not directly related to the school work. Said official shall strictly adjust himself to these rules in considering petitions on the use of the schoolrooms and other school properties for such purposes. Furthermore, the school superintendent shall notify the principal of the building of any permission granted, in order that he take the necessary measures for the protection of the school property under his charge. The grantee of each one of these permissions shall be responsible, on his own account, for repairing any damages that may occur to the school property on the occasion of the holding of the activity authorized thereby, also for the payment of the electricity, water, cleaning or of any other services used or expenses in relation to said activity. 

§ 102-5. Interference with school 

No permission shall be granted that will interrupt the school work day or night -or that might endanger the property, or the dignity and decorum of the school building.

Therefore, the Secretary of Education may refuse any order sent for his approval after the expenditure has been made. (d) The allowance for the purchase of materials shall be used by the school director and the superintendent of schools for all kinds of materials and goods of educational character used in any branch of teaching; for materials of cleanliness in general; for materials and spare parts in relation to repair work of equipment and buildings and for office materials and desk supplies. The school director and the superintendent of schools shall jointly distribute the total sum allocated for materials, taking into consideration the relative needs of the schools of different classes and of different branches of teaching, as well as the offices, school dependencies and establishments in general, so that the benefit of that overall allowance covers, proportionally and insofar as possible, everybody. § 104-5. School property 

(a) The superintendents of schools shall continue in their respective districts to be in charge of the custody and local accountability of all the school property, therefore they shall be responsible to the property official in the central office. (b) The inspection and surveillance of the school buildings shall be exercised together by both the school director and the superintendent of schools. The school director may visit and inspect said buildings with the necessary frequency and make pertinent recommendations for the protection, maintenance and improvement of same. (c) The use of buildings and other school property for purposes other than those of teaching shall be permitted only through the express consent of the competent authority and subject strictly to the regulations in effect on that matter [§§ 102-1 to 102-5], which regulations, policies and instructions shall become a part hereof. 142

§ 105-1. Importance 

The old theory that the janitor is only a simple sweeper, has been completely discarded. Many educators consider the janitor as an important factor in the functioning of the school. Precisely, through the particular class of services which he is called upon to render, which are several and important, it is necessary to classify persons. The relations of these employees with the school, must be appraised under the following aspects, which are mainly: 

(1) Custody of the property 

(2) Domestic work proper to the school (3) Moral influence (4) Elementary principles of hygiene and wholesomeness (5) Safety of the students (6) Education and physical condition

An exemplary janitor should be endowed with conditions that will effectively allow him to fulfill his obligations under such conditions and always in accordance with and obedient to the orders of his superiors, especially with those of the school principal. 143

T.§ 105-1 Ch. 7 

 Source. §§ 105-1 to 105-8: Rules and regulations of Depart ment of Education, app. by Secretary of Education, Vol. I, pp. 52 to 54, "School Janitors". (Circular Letter No. 206 of 

June 30, 1947), app. June 24, 1947, eff. July 1, 1947. Filed with Secretary of State Sept. 28, 1957; File No. 344. 

§§ 105-9 to 105-14: See note under section 104-1. 

Authority. Act Mar. 19, 1946, No. 76, p. 166; 18 L.P.R.A. 

§ 105. 

§ 105-2. Guardian of property 

The janitor should be a true and diligent guardian of the school property, placed under his care, against all risks or dangers. 

§ 105-3. Janitor as example 

In the execution of the domestic labors proper of the school every janitor shall serve as an example of cleanliness and good taste, so that his work induces good habits in the minds of the students who still lack them, and through them conveying same to their homes, and helping those who have such good habits in retaining them.

The janitor should also show neatness and correctness in the dress and shoes that he wears. Under no circumstances should he be allowed to be barefooted within the school. 

§ 105-4. Character 

The position of a janitor is no place for a person of uncertain reputation or of doubtful integrity. Through the schools all the generations of citizens pass at the most critical age; and there more than at any other place they should be surrounded by healthy moral influences. 

§ 105-5. Sanitary conditions 

The janitor should have a clear notion of the rules and hygienic principles applicable to the maintaining of the buildings in good sanitary condition. 

§ 105-6. Safety 

The janitor, as much as the teachers, shall look after the safety of the students and shall be an efficient assistant thereof in the organization of the entrance and exit exercises, in the recess periods, in the school lunchroom and in every sort of activity outside the schoolrooms. 144

Ch. T.18 § 105-10 

§ 105-7. Literacy; health; work load

The janitor should be a person who knows how to read and write, since it would be anomalous to employ an illiterate for school service, for this kind of work. Furthermore, the work of this employee requires that his physical condition and state of health be absolutely satisfactory.

On the other hand, work superior to his physical strength should not be required from the janitor, making him look after an excessive number of rooms. This number shall be such as will allow him to attend all the rooms efficiently and maintain them absolutely clean and in order. 

§ 105-8. Local regulations 

In every municipality a local regulation shall be adopted and put into effect for the service of janitors, based on the preceding provisions. 

§ 105-9. Appointment Pursuant to Act No. 472 [18 L.P.R.A. § 105], the appointment of school janitors shall be made by the Secretary of Education on proposal of the mayor, and for that purpose the law has excluded them from the Classified Civil Service. § 105-10. Vacancies; notice; candidates 

On and after July 1, 1947, the vacancies for janitors in schools shall be notified immediately by the superintendent of schools to the respective mayor, using the Form A.E.M.-6, which shall be filled out in quintuplicate, the original and three copies thereof to be sent to the municipal official, and the other copy being held to be filed. In the corresponding blank spaces of the same model form the mayor shall set forth the names of the candidates recommended to fill the vacancies, returning the original and two copies to the superintendent of schools and keeping for himself one of the copies. The original and the two copies received from the mayor shall be sent by the superintendent of schools to the Secretary of Education, together with an application for employment that every candidate shall fill out in Form A.E.M.-7. If the proposal of the mayor is approved, the Secretary of Education shall sign and return copies of same to the mayor and superintendent of schools, respectively. In case of disapproval, the proposal shall be returned to the mayor with the pertinent objection. 145

T.§ 105-11 Ch. 7 

 § 105-11. Appointment forms; disposition 

Together with each proposal approved by the Secretary of Education there shall be sent to the superintendent of schools the corresponding appointment for each candidate, as well as the model form for the taking of oath, physical examination and personal history of the candidate which shall be executed by the appointed persons before commencing employment. All the copies of these documents (oath, physical examination and personal record) shall be returned, once they are executed, to the Department of Education for further proceedings. The superintendent of schools shall be responsible for the restitution of these documents. 

§ 105-12. Qualifications of janitors 

Every candidate recommended by the mayor shall meet all the qualifications and requirements established by secs. 105-1 to 105-8. 

§ 105-13. Supervision 

The janitors as well as all the personnel transferred from the Municipal Government to the Insular Government as an effect of 

Act 76 of 1946 [18 L.P.R.A. §§ 101 to 105], as well as the per sonnel appointed by the Secretary of Education to render services in the school districts, shall discharge their duties and shall exercise their functions under the immediate direction and supervision of the respective superintendents of schools. § 105-14. Suspension; dismissal

The school janitors or other school employees may be suspended from employment and pay and dismissed from office, through due procedure, by reason of turpitude, neglect in fulfilment of their duties, insubordination, incompetency, cruelty or any other misconduct. The suspension or dismissal, in such case, shall be resolved by the Secretary of Education. Whenever the superintendent of schools may have cognizance that a janitor or other employee has committed any of the faults above mentioned, he shall report the case, with his recommendations, to the Secretary of Education, who shall direct that an investigation be made to determine if there is cause for any actionfi and if so to proceed accordingly. 146

§ 126-11. Definitions 

For the purposes of this division, it shall be understood by: (1) "School building", any structure with all other annex property under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Education; (2) "Political party", any party recognized and registered as such under the Law of Inscriptions and Elections of Puerto Rico [16 L.P.R.A. § 1 et seq.], and thus enabled to nominate candidates and to participate in the election process; (3) "Profit producing activities”, activities that produce an economic or pecuniary gain with the exception of those activities whose economic product is totally used for the benefit of the school; (4) "Activity of a sectarian character", activity with aims related to any religious or sectarian denomination; 

Aug. 31, 1968 

Vol. 7, No. 8 146.1

T.§ 126-11 Ch. 7 

EDUCATION-PUBLIC SCHOOLS 

(5) "Activity of a politically partisan character", activities sponsored by any number of persons that advocate for certain governmental ideas or maintain certain political principles or beliefs in public policies of government which advance the achievement of the purposes or goals of the group; (6) "Internal instrumentalities", the central, municipal and ward (barrio) committees of a political party.

Source. Sections 126-11 to 126-21: Rules and Regulations Governing the Use of School Buildings, app. by the Secretary of Public Education Aug. 1, 1968, eff. 30 days after being filed with the Secretary of State. Filed with the Secretary of State Aug. 13, 1968; File No. 1198. Published in the

Puerto Rico Register Aug. 31, 1968; Vol. 7, No. 8. 

Authority. Act April 24, 1961, No. 4, p. 31; 18 L.P.R.A. 

§ 126. 

Repeals. Section 11 of Rules and Regulations, File No. 

1198, set out in this division, provided: "All rules and regulations, provisions or norms in conflict herewith, are hereby repealed."

Introduction. Rules and Regulations, File No. 1198, set out in this division, contained the following introduction: 

"Act No. 4 of April 24, 1961, as amended by Act No. 3 

of March 20, 1963, authorizes the Secretary of Public Education to grant the free use of school buildings to public or private entities, groups or associations, recognized as such, for the holding of public functions, meetings and civic or cultural activities 'not having profitable purposes or politically partisan or sectarian character'. This latter restriction is, by the same statute, pronounced inapplicable to: "1. Voting for the nomination, by members of a political party, of candidates for a) elective offices b) offices in its internal instrumentalities; "2. Training, on the part of political parties, of officers in charge of election of primary polling places; "3. Holding of primaries and further procedures pertaining thereto, both on the part of political parties or the Institute of Primaries. 

"Said legislation further vests in the Secretary of Public Education the authority to establish the necessary rules and regulations to carry into effect its purposes and provisions. "In the exercise of that authority and for the proper performance of the facultative functions conferred upon by the aforesaid legislation, the Secretary of Public Education hereby establishes these ***.” 

Cross references. Private use of school buildings and other school properties, see also § 102–1 et seq. of this title. 

Aug. 31, 1968 

Vol. 7, No. 8 146.2

Ch. T.18 § 126-16 

 § 126-12. Hourly schedule 

The use of school buildings for the purposes authorized by this division and by the law supporting the same [18 L.P.R.A. § 126] shall be granted only for activities to be held outside of the hourly schedule of the educational work for which the buildings are primarily assigned. 

§ 126-13. Applications-Authorized officials 

The superintendents of schools, in their respective districts, shall be the officials designated by the Secretary of Public Education to receive, pass upon, approve or deny the applications for the aforesaid purposes as submitted to them by the parties in interest. 

§ 126-14. Place for filing 

Every public or private entity, group or association, recognized as such, which is interested in being granted permission to use the school buildings for holding functions, meetings or other activities of a civic or a cultural character, of public concern and devoid of profitable, politically partisan or sectarian purposes, shall submit the respective application to the superintendent of schools of the district where the building which is the subject of the same is located, by filling therefore the application blank which will be supplied by said school official. 

§ 126-15. -Political parties 

Every political party, as well as the Institute of Primaries, when interested in using the school buildings for any of the political purposes authorized by law, as they appear described and enumerated in the introduction to this division, shall present the respective application, following the same procedure set forth in sec. 126–14 of this title. § 126-16. When must be filed 

The application referred to in the preceding sections shall be made 15 days in advance of the date set for holding the activity and shall be signed by an official or authorized agent of the applying entity, who has the power to undertake in behalf thereof the responsibilities and obligations concomitant of the application, such as taking diligent care of the school property, repairing damage caused thereto and cleaning the premises used. The applying entity shall further take necessary measures leading to an appropriate 

Aug. 31, 1968 

Vol. 7, No. 8 146.3

T.18 126 Ch. 7 

EDUCATION-PUBLIC SCHOOLS 

organization and to maintaining order, in connection with the activity to be held. 

§ 126-17. Decision and notification 

The superintendent of schools shall study every application for the use of school buildings under the provisions of this division, shall decide upon it according to its merits, and shall make his decision known to the applicant within the 5 day period subsequent to receiving the application. In case of doubt with respect to the interpretation of the provisions of this division, the superintendent of schools will consult the Secretary of Public Education, by submitting the matter to him within the same period of 5 days. 

Denial The application shall be denied by the superintendent of schools in any of the following cases: (1) When the activities to be held are for profitable purposes, or call for the purchase of admission tickets or any other form of payment to attend them. This restriction shall not be construed as applicable to the activities of public or private organization when the product thereof is totally devoted for the benefit of the school; (2) When the activities are politically partisan or sectarian in character, or are sponsored by any party or group of a politically partisan or sectarian nature or character, and do not belong in such exceptional political activities as are authorized by law and which appear described and enumerated in the introduction to this division; (3) When it would appear certain that the activities, on account of their duration, will impede the subsequent conditioning of rooms and other accessories for resuming classes and other school exercises; (4) When the holding of the activity is, or when there is a well founded risk that it will be, related in any way with the dispensing or any other form of distribution of alcoholic beverages, in the building or its surroundings. 

§ 126-19. Appeal 

The resolution of the superintendent of schools denying the use of school buildings shall be appealable by the loser, at least 5 days in advance of the date set for holding the activity, before the Secre- 

Aug. 31, 1968 

Vol. 7, No. 8 146.4

Ch. T.18 § 126-21 

tary of Public Education who after hearing the parties will decide the case, and his decision will be final. 

§ 126-20. Supervision 

The superintendent of schools shall see to it that the conditions set down for granting the use of the school are strictly complied with; and he shall likewise have the power, because of the violation of any of those conditions, to revoke the grant and to order the building vacated. Furthermore, he shall have the power to deny future concessions of the use of school buildings to any concessionary that has violated the provisions of this division. 

§ 126-21. Effectiveness 

This division shall become effective 30 days after being filed with the Secretary of State of Puerto Rico, according to law.

Chapter 9. Textbooks Subchapter 153. Accountability for Textbooks

Forms § 153-1. Purpose 

There are hereby established the following regulations to enforce the provision of Act No. 102 of April 18, 1952 [18 L.P.R.A. § 153]. This Act empowers the Secretary of Education to relieve the school directors and teachers from the payment for books lost, up to five per cent of the total number of books distributed. 

Source. §§ 153-1 to 153-8: Rules and regulations of Depart ment of Education, app. by Secretary of Education, Vol. I, pp. 104 to 106, "Regulation to enforce the provisions of Act 

No. 102 of April 18, 1952 on textbooks". Filed with Secretary of State Sept. 28, 1957; File No. 344. 

Authority. Act Apr. 18, 1952, No. 102, p. 206; 18 L.P.R.A. 

§ 153. 

§ 153-2. Account of loss 

The principals, or school directors and the teachers shall be relieved from the obligation to pay or replace the books which might be lost annually, up to a maximum of 5% (five per cent) of the total number of books under their custody. The payment or replacement shall be accounted by titles separately and on the basis of the books distributed for the use of teachers and pupils, when the loss occurs while the books are in the possession of the teachers or pupils. In the latter case there shall be obtained from the parents or guardian a statement verifying such loss. 

§ 153-3. Reports 

The teacher shall take note of the books lost, and upon the termination of the school year, or when he ceases to fulfill his office, he shall make a report stating the number of books lost and giving in detail the titles and the amounts involved therein, as well as the names of the pupils responsible for the loss. The report shall be made in triplicate and shall be sent to the proper 147

T.§ 153-3 

Ch. 9

school director or assistant superintendent, as the case may be, together with a credited statement signed by the parents or guardian of the pupils. After the books have been classified as old and new books, the teacher shall only specify the unit price of same and the total amount of the items or titles where the loss is over the 5% of the exempt payment. This report shall be made in the form titled Report of Books Lost (Revised). 

The Director or assistant superintendent shall render to the superintendent of schools a brief report specifying the loss of books distributed to the teachers under his direction and occurring in the course of the school year, using for such purpose the above mentioned form. § 153-4. Old books, payment

There shall be considered as old books those which are rustic, paper or board bound which have been used for a year, and the cloth bound books after two years of use. The new books shall be paid for according to the price list and the old ones at half their price. 

§ 153-5. Inventory 

For the purpose of dropping from the inventory of each district the books lost during the school year the superintendent of schools shall render (at the end of that year) a report in triplicate specifying the books lost in his district with the amount of the books paid, if any. This report shall include the books lost exempt from payment up to the 5%, and, in addition, the books paid by the teachers and directors. There shall be indicated in the form on 

Report for Lost Books (Revised) the price of the books and the total amount. 

§ 153-6. File of report 

The reports of lost books submitted by each teacher and district director and the credited statement of lost books signed by the parents or guardians of the pupils, shall be filed in the office of the superintendent of schools at the end of the year, and shall be at all times available to be inspected by the competent officials of the school system and of the Government of Puerto Rico. § 153-7. Loss without fault

The loss of books caused by cyclones, fires, thefts or similar causes, shall be credited, according to the proceeding established 148

Ch. T.18 § 153-8 

TEXTBOOKS 

for these cases in the law and in the regulation on accountability and control of public property. Those lost shall be reported separately from those comprised under Act No. 102 of 1952 [18 

L.P.R.A. § 153]. 

§ 153-8. Forms 

For the credited statement of parents or guardians and the report of the directors or teachers to which secs. 153–4, 153–5, and 153-6 of this title, respectively, refer to, shall be used the model forms attached herewith.

The new regulation, as it may be seen, provides a definite proceeding to account for the 5% exempt payment for lost books and to prepare the report that the superintendent of schools. shall render to the Department of Education at the end of the school year. So that the preparation of the report is simplified, both for the Division of Finance of the Department of Education as well as for the office of the superintendent of schools proper, the 5% exemption in the payment for books shall only be applicable to books distributed for the use of the pupils and of the teachers and shall be made separately by titles of books. Therefore, books in stock or pending confiscation are not included. 

These amendments respond to the purpose of the law and to our interest in obtaining a better and effective distribution of the books for the benefit of the pupils and teachers.

183-15. General rules 

§ 183-1. Objectives 

Objectives of this division are: (1) To further and generalize the use of the procedure of regulated and controlled demand, offer and acceptance of products, with a view to a sound and free competition among the largest number of bidders. (2) Obtain the utmost benefit from the funds sent by the School Lunchroom Division or secured locally, as a result of reduced prices and improved quality and variety of the products. (3) Comply with the requirements established by the existing laws and regulations of the Government of the Commonwealth of 

Puerto Rico on this matter. 

(4) Inform the public about the details of the investments of 

Treasury funds. (5) Achieve a speedier and more efficient delivery to lunchrooms of all necessary local products.

Source. §§ 183-1 to 183-15: Rules and regulations of Department of Education, Vol. II, Circular Letter No. 13, on procedure governing the purchase of foodstuffs and supplies in school districts through bids and in open market, for use of school lunchrooms, app. by Secretary of Education, Aug. 

25, 1954; Memo. No. 7, Oct. 18, 1954, Manual of Procedure "Procurement and Receipt of Products in School Districts".
